explain.say: Power stations must make exactly as much electricity as we use, moment by moment. Baseload stations, like nuclear plants, run steadily day and night to cover the minimum demand that is always there.

explain.say: Demand is lowest at night, rises in the morning and peaks in the early evening, when people get home, cook and switch on lights. Baseload fills the bottom of this curve and peakers fill the top.

Baseload plants cost a lot to build but have cheap fuel, so they pay off by running all the time. Peakers are cheaper to build but costly to run, so they work only a few hours. Wind and solar add a third kind: whatever the weather gives.

faq.a: Baseload is the lowest level of electricity demand through the day, which never goes away, and the power stations that run nonstop to supply it. Nuclear and geothermal plants are classic baseload stations.

faq.q: What is a peaking power station?
faq.a: A peaker is a power station that only runs when demand is highest, sometimes for just a few hundred hours a year. Gas turbines, hydro dams and big batteries make good peakers because they start fast.

faq.q: Why can't nuclear power stations follow demand easily?
faq.a: Nuclear plants can change output, and French ones do, but slowly and with extra wear. Their fuel is cheap and the building very expensive, so it usually makes most sense to run them flat out.
asks: Can nuclear power go up and down?

faq.a: In Britain demand peaks on winter weekday evenings, roughly 5 to 7 pm, when lighting, cooking and heating overlap. In hot countries the peak often comes on summer afternoons from air conditioning.
asks: What time do people use the most electricity?

faq.q: Where do wind and solar fit in?
faq.a: Wind and solar make electricity whenever the weather allows, at very low running cost, so the grid uses all it can. Other power stations and storage then fill the gaps when the wind drops or the sun sets.

facts: Some peaking gas turbines run for only a few hundred hours a year.
France gets around two thirds of its electricity from nuclear power and adjusts reactor output to follow demand.
